problem: Existing navigation methods treat the robot as a 2D point mass, and combining separate navigation and manipulation stacks leaves humanoids without coordinated whole-body navigation and reaching. End-to-end training would need heterogeneous data with both egocentric vision and full-body motion.
motivation: Any manipulation task starts with delivering hands and cameras to the right place in human-designed 3D spaces. The paper decouples egocentric perception from physical action through a 3-point (eyes, two hands) interface, so each part can learn from a different, more available human data source.
key_idea: Use head and two-hand 6D pose targets as the interface between a high-level vision policy (trained on Aria-glasses human data plus a little robot data) and a low-level whole-body controller (trained by adversarial imitation RL on mocap).
insight: Whole-body tracking of sparse 3-point targets works only with discriminators: with none, failure is 97% in Isaac Gym, and splitting into upper- and lower-body discriminators halves the position error versus a single one (0.075 vs 0.149 m). For navigation, robot data is needed to close the embodiment gap (H-Lab only SR 0.14 vs R-Lab 0.71), while large out-of-distribution human data (ADT) and in-domain human data help generalization to new scenes (kitchen SR 0.35 to 0.60). A shared decoder for human and robot data beats a two-branch one (kitchen SR 0.60 vs 0.20).
method: Whole-body controller: single-stage PPO with ICCGAN-style discriminator ensembles (32 each) plus a goal-directed reward tracks 6D poses of eyes, left hand and right hand on the Unitree G1. It runs at 30Hz with PD servos and uses multi-objective advantage weights of 0.2/0.2/0.6.
Two discriminators: separate imitation rewards for the arm group and the torso/lower-body group, so the policy can combine motions from different clips (e.g. walk without arm swing while carrying).

Deployable observation: local link poses over two frames, joint velocity and root angular velocity, with targets as relative transforms. No world-frame root position or velocity is used. Action delay and dynamics randomization aid sim-to-real.
Motion data: 1363 clips (~5 h) from AMASS and OMOMO retargeted to the G1 by keypoint matching.

Navigation module: DINO features of the RGB image plus a positional embedding of the 2D goal go to a transformer decoder that predicts the future camera trajectory. The goal is tracked across frames with CoTracker3.

Human data pipeline: Aria glasses give camera poses, point clouds and gaze, and the goal is the gaze ray's intersection with the point cloud projected into the image. Fisheye is undistorted and a pitch homography is applied to mimic the robot camera, and human clips are subsampled for the ~7x speed gap. The model is co-trained on human, ADT (400 min) and a small amount of mocap-recorded robot data.

Reaching module: a second downward RGB-D camera; the goal is transferred by LoFTR matching, lifted to a 3D hand target, and Mink IK infers head pose and hand orientation with CoM and pelvis regularization.

setting.backbone: DINO features + transformer decoder (navigation, trained); PPO/GAN-based whole-body policy (trained from scratch); CoTracker3, LoFTR and Mink IK as off-the-shelf components
setting.training_data: WBC: ~5 h retargeted AMASS+OMOMO mocap (1363 clips). Navigation: 200 Aria human clips per room (~4 s each), ADT 400 min, 24 robot lab clips (~30 s each) from mocap.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB from a wide webcam (90° HFOV) for navigation, a downward RGB-D camera (RealSense D435) for reaching, proprioception
setting.action_space: 3-point (head, left hand, right hand) 6D pose targets at high level; 27-DoF joint targets via PD at low level
setting.simulator: Isaac Gym (WBC training), MuJoCo (sim2sim), real world
setting.privileged: Mocap markers on the robot head give world-frame closed-loop tracking during real-world experiments; the user provides the goal point in the initial image.

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is used. Lab success is 10/12 and kitchen 7/12 from Table real_eval; the text's '25% greater' matches the lab-kitchen gap. Navigation SR and Error are open-loop prediction metrics, not closed-loop navigation.
results: The real-robot system reaches 71% success across two rooms with unseen layouts and objects, and the lab room is about 25% higher than the kitchen. Ablations show that mixing robot data, in-domain human data and ADT gives the best navigation (lab SR 0.86, kitchen SR 0.60 vs 0.35 zero-shot with robot data only). Two discriminators beat a single one (MuJoCo failure 3% vs 13%).
limitations: Only head and wrist poses are controlled, so the robot takes conservative paths and does not use full-body maneuvers such as sidestepping or stepping over obstacles; the 3-point interface is also ambiguous for the lower body (bend vs walk), causing hesitation.
Real-world evaluation is small (6 layouts × 4 objects) and needs mocap for world-frame closed-loop tracking; the goal tracker fails with motion blur and reflective surfaces.
Human data is faster and more aggressive than the robot can follow, which causes collisions; navigation is evaluated open-loop on small clip sets.
